issues.legal_issue: A court may draw an adverse inference from a party’s withholding of evidence only after assessing its relevance and the parties’ pleadings, burdens, and diligence, including whether the opposing party sought its production through the available procedure.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought inspection of government records from authorities controlled by the defendant but was not permitted to inspect them.
The plaintiff did not seek interrogatories, inspection, or production through the prescribed court procedure, and no court order directing production was made.
The appellate courts drew an adverse inference against the defendant for not producing the records.
issues.conclusion: The appellate courts were not entitled to draw an adverse inference against the defendant on these facts.
issues.legal_principle: Section 114(g) of the Evidence Act makes an adverse inference discretionary, not automatic. The court must consider the relevance of withheld evidence, the burden of proof, the other party’s diligence and available discovery procedures, and any explanation for non-production. The Court relied on Murugesam Pillai v. Gnana Sambandha Pandara Sannadhi, Gopal Krishnaji Ketkar v. Mohamed Haji Latif, Kamma Otukunta Ram Naidu v. Chereddy Pedda Subba Reddy, Municipal Corporation, Faridabad v. Siri Niwas, Mahant Shri Srinivas Ramanuj Das v. Surjanarayan Das, Ramrati Kuer v. Dwarika Prasad Singh, and the discovery and inspection procedures in Order XI CPC.

rule.if: civil_title_proceeding and evidence_is_held_by_opposing_party and opposing_party_did_not_seek_production_through_available_procedure and no_court_order_to_produce_was_disobeyed

predicates.civil_title_proceeding: A party brings a civil proceeding to establish title to property.
predicates.evidence_is_held_by_opposing_party: Material evidence relevant to the dispute is held by the opposing party.
predicates.opposing_party_did_not_seek_production_t: The party seeking the evidence does not use the available procedure to request its production or inspection.
predicates.no_court_order_to_produce_was_disobeyed: The court has not ordered the holder to produce the evidence, or the holder has complied with any such order.

issues.definition: When a party seeking relevant evidence does not use the available production procedure and no production order is disobeyed, the court is not justified in drawing an adverse inference merely because the opposing party holds the evidence.

issues.legal_issue: A party’s failure to produce a document in rebuttal does not, by itself, amount to an admission of that document or its contents.
material_facts: The plaintiff produced a Will during the first appeal as additional evidence.
The defendant did not produce a document in rebuttal after the Will was taken on record.
The first appellate court treated the absence of rebuttal evidence as an admission of the Will and its contents, although no admission had been made through the applicable procedure.
issues.conclusion: The first appellate court erred in treating the defendant’s failure to produce rebuttal evidence as an admission of the Will or its contents.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 17–31 and 58 of the Evidence Act govern admissions; Section 58 dispenses with proof only where a fact is admitted at or before the hearing in the manner contemplated by that provision. Order XII CPC provides procedures for admissions of cases and documents. A failure to prove a defence does not amount to an admission or shift the plaintiff’s burden. The Court relied on Nagubai Ammal v. B. Shama Rao, L.I.C. of India v. Ram Pal Singh Bisen, and other authorities on admissions.

predicates.civil_proceeding: The dispute is being decided in a civil proceeding.
predicates.a_party_relies_on_a_document: One party relies on a document to establish a fact in dispute.
predicates.the_opposing_party_does_not_produce_rebu: The opposing party does not produce evidence to rebut the document.
predicates.no_admission_was_made_through_the_applic: The opposing party has not admitted the document or its contents through a recognized written, pleading, or hearing procedure.

issues.definition: In a civil proceeding, the opposing party’s failure to rebut a relied-on document is not an admission when that party has not admitted it through the applicable procedure.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may receive additional evidence only within the conditions governing that power, and an application decided before the appeal is heard on its merits cannot be used to establish that the evidence is required for judgment.
material_facts: The plaintiff applied during the first appeal to add a Will as evidence.
The first appellate court allowed the application before hearing the appeal on its merits.
The order allowing the application did not assess at the merits hearing whether the appellate court required the evidence to pronounce judgment or for another substantial cause.
The Will was central to a claim not pleaded in the plaint and was not proved in the required manner.
issues.conclusion: The order admitting the Will, made before the hearing on the merits, was to be ignored; the Will could not be relied on to decide the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Order XLI Rule 27 CPC permits additional evidence only in the specified circumstances, including where the appellate court requires it to pronounce judgment or for another substantial cause. The power is judicial, exceptional, and not a right to repair a party’s case; the application is considered at the hearing on the merits after assessing the existing record, and reasons should be recorded. The Court relied on K. Venkataramiah v. A. Seetharama Reddy, The Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay v. Lala Pancham, Haji Mohammed Ishaq v. Mohamed Iqbal, Arjan Singh v. Kartar Singh, and Parsotim Thakur v. Lal Mohar Thakur.

rule.if: appellate_proceeding and additional_evidence_is_requested and (application_is_decided_before_merits_hearing or evidence_was_available_below_without_satisfactory_cause or appellate_court_does_not_require_evidence_to_decide_the_case)

predicates.appellate_proceeding: A court is hearing an appeal from a lower court’s decision.
predicates.additional_evidence_is_requested: A party asks the appellate court to add evidence that was not part of the lower court’s record.
predicates.application_is_decided_before_merits_hea: The appellate court decides whether to admit the evidence before hearing the appeal on its merits.
predicates.evidence_was_available_below_without_sat: The party had a fair opportunity to present the evidence below and has not shown a satisfactory reason for failing to do so.
predicates.appellate_court_does_not_require_evidenc: The appellate court can decide the appeal on the existing record and does not require the proposed evidence for judgment or another substantial cause.

issues.definition: In an appeal, requested additional evidence cannot be relied on if its admission is decided before the merits hearing, it could have been presented below without satisfactory cause, or the appellate court does not require it to decide the case.

issues.legal_issue: A court cannot grant relief based on a factual claim that is not supported by the pleadings, and evidence directed to that unpleaded claim cannot establish it.
material_facts: The plaint asserted inheritance through the plaintiff’s family history but did not rely on a Will as the source of title.
The pleadings were not amended to introduce a claim based on the Will.
The first appellate court relied heavily on the Will to find title, although the Will had not been pleaded and had not been proved as required for a Will.
issues.conclusion: The Will could not be relied on to establish the plaintiff’s title because the claim based on it was not pleaded; it was also not proved in accordance with law.
issues.legal_principle: A decision must be founded on the parties’ pleadings, and evidence outside those pleadings cannot ordinarily be relied on to grant relief. Section 68 of the Evidence Act governs proof of a Will requiring attestation. The Court relied on Kalyan Singh Chouhan v. C.P. Joshi and Bachhaj Nahar v. Nilima Mandal, among other authorities on pleadings and proof.

predicates.civil_proceeding: The dispute is being decided in a civil proceeding.
predicates.a_party_relies_on_evidence_to_establish_: A party relies on evidence as the basis for a claimed right or relief.
predicates.the_claim_is_not_supported_by_pleadings: The pleadings do not set out the material factual basis of the claim.
predicates.the_pleadings_were_not_amended_to_raise_: The party does not amend the pleadings to introduce that factual basis.

issues.definition: Evidence cannot establish a claim in a civil proceeding when the claim’s factual basis is absent from the pleadings and the pleadings are not amended to include it.

issues.legal_issue: A suit seeking only a declaration of title is not maintainable when the plaintiff is out of possession and omits to seek available consequential relief.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought a declaration of ownership of the land but did not seek possession or another consequential relief.
The plaintiff was admittedly not in possession of the land.
issues.conclusion: The suit was barred because the plaintiff sought a declaration without seeking consequential relief despite not being in possession.
issues.legal_principle: The proviso to Section 34 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 prevents a court from granting a declaration where the plaintiff, being able to seek further relief, omits to do so. The Court relied on Ram Saran v. Smt. Ganga Devi, Vinay Krishna v. Keshav Chandra, and Gian Kaur v. Raghubir Singh.

rule.if: declaratory_suit and plaintiff_is_out_of_possession and plaintiff_can_seek_consequential_relief and plaintiff_does_not_seek_consequential_relief

predicates.declaratory_suit: The plaintiff brings a suit seeking a declaration of a right or status.
predicates.plaintiff_is_out_of_possession: The plaintiff is not in possession of the property in dispute.
predicates.plaintiff_can_seek_consequential_relief: The plaintiff is able to seek relief in addition to a declaration, such as recovery of possession.
predicates.plaintiff_does_not_seek_consequential_re: The plaintiff asks only for a declaration and omits available additional relief.

issues.definition: A declaratory suit is not maintainable when the plaintiff is out of possession, can seek consequential relief, and omits to seek it.

issues.legal_issue: In a title claim, the claimant bears the burden of proving the claimant’s own title, and a failure by the opposing party to prove its title does not discharge that burden.
material_facts: The plaintiff claimed ownership through an alleged historic grant, family succession, and partition.
The trial court found that the plaintiff had not proved the family pedigree, the alleged grant, or the alleged partition.
The appellate courts shifted the burden to the government because it had not proved its own title, although the plaintiff’s title was the issue to be determined.
The plaintiff’s other asserted evidence did not establish title.
issues.conclusion: The appellate courts erred in shifting the burden to the government; the plaintiff failed to prove title and could not succeed merely because the government’s title had not been proved.
issues.legal_principle: The party making a factual averment bears the burden of proving it. A claimant seeking title must establish that title; failure to prove an opposing defence does not amount to an admission or reverse the claimant’s burden. The Court applied the principles in Section 114(g) of the Evidence Act and relied on L.I.C. of India v. Ram Pal Singh Bisen and authorities concerning burden of proof.

predicates.civil_title_proceeding: A party brings a civil proceeding to establish ownership of property.
predicates.claimant_asserts_ownership: The claimant asserts a right of ownership in the disputed property.
predicates.claimant_does_not_prove_the_material_bas: The claimant fails to prove the facts or evidence on which the asserted title depends.
predicates.the_decision_maker_treats_opponent_failu: The decision-maker treats the opposing party’s failure to establish its own title as enough to find for the claimant.

issues.definition: In a civil title proceeding, a claimant who fails to prove the basis of ownership has not established title merely because the opposing party also failed to prove title.

issues.legal_issue: The age of a document may support a presumption about its execution and attestation, but it does not by itself prove the truth of its contents or that those contents were acted upon.
material_facts: The plaintiff relied on an alleged historic partition among ancestors to support title.
The plaintiff’s family pedigree was not proved.
The Court explained that even if the alleged partition had occurred, it did not establish the plaintiff’s title on the evidence in the case.
issues.conclusion: The age of an old document did not establish the truth of its contents or prove the plaintiff’s title.
issues.legal_principle: Section 90 of the Evidence Act permits a presumption concerning the signature, execution, and attestation of a document that is at least thirty years old and comes from proper custody. It does not presume that every statement in the document is correct or that the document was acted upon; those matters must be proved as facts.

predicates.civil_title_proceeding: A party brings a civil proceeding to establish ownership of property.
predicates.a_party_relies_on_an_old_document_from_p: A party relies on a document old enough to attract an age-based presumption and produced from proper custody.
predicates.the_party_uses_the_document_to_prove_the: The party relies on statements in the document as proof that those statements are true or were acted upon.

issues.definition: In a civil title proceeding, an old document from proper custody does not, by age alone, prove the truth of its contents.

issues.legal_issue: Certified copies of official land-register records maintained under the applicable land-administration system are admissible public documents, and their entries are conclusive evidence of title.
material_facts: The government produced certified extracts from an official land register identifying the disputed land as government land managed by a military estate officer.
The appellate courts rejected the certified entries and did not properly appreciate them.
issues.conclusion: The appellate courts erred in rejecting the certified land-register records; the records were admissible and their entries were conclusive evidence of title.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 65 and 74 of the Evidence Act permit certified copies of public documents to be admitted in evidence. The Court held that entries in the General Land Register maintained under the Cantonment Land Administration Rules are conclusive evidence of title, relying on Chief Executive Officer v. Surendra Kumar Vakil and Union of India v. Kamla Verma.

predicates.title_proceeding: The dispute concerns ownership of land.
predicates.a_certified_copy_of_an_official_land_reg: A party offers a certified copy of an official register containing entries about the disputed land.
predicates.the_register_is_maintained_as_a_public_r: The register is maintained as an official public record under the land-administration system governing the land.

issues.definition: In a title proceeding, entries in a properly maintained official land register are admissible and conclusive evidence of title when a certified copy is tendered.

issues.legal_issue: A second appellate court must address the substantial questions of law framed for decision unless it decides the appeal on another ground or determines that the framed questions are not substantial questions of law.
material_facts: The High Court framed substantial questions of law, including questions concerning the additional Will, the land-register records, and the maintainability of the declaratory suit.
The High Court did not answer the framed questions or determine that they were not substantial questions of law.
The unresolved questions affected the result of the appeal.
issues.conclusion: The High Court committed a grave error by failing to address the framed substantial questions of law.
issues.legal_principle: Section 100 CPC confines a second appeal to substantial questions of law. A second appellate court must answer the questions framed unless the appeal is finally decided on one or more of them or the court concludes that a framed question is not substantial; additional substantial questions may be framed when necessary. The Court relied on State Bank of India v. S.N. Goyal, Vijay Kumar Talwar v. Commissioner of Income Tax, and the principles governing substantial questions of law.

rule.if: second_appeal and substantial_questions_of_law_are_framed and the_high_court_does_not_answer_them and the_high_court_does_not_decide_the_appeal_on_another_ground

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding is a second appeal from an appellate court’s decision.
predicates.substantial_questions_of_law_are_framed: The court identifies substantial questions of law for determination in the appeal.
predicates.the_high_court_does_not_answer_them: The court gives no decision on the framed substantial questions.
predicates.the_high_court_does_not_decide_the_appea: The court does not finally resolve the appeal on another question or determine that the framed questions are not substantial.

issues.definition: A second appellate decision is legally defective when the court leaves framed substantial questions unanswered without finally resolving the appeal on another ground.

issues.legal_issue: A vague, undated rent note that does not identify the property, the parties, the lease term, or the rent period cannot establish title.
material_facts: A rent note referred generally to land and rent of twenty-two rupees but did not describe the disputed property or state its date, the parties to the lease, the lease duration, or the period for which rent was payable.
The note did not bear a lessee’s signature or thumb impression.
The plaint did not refer to the rent note, and the note could not be linked to the disputed land in the circumstances.
issues.conclusion: The rent note was too vague to establish title and was to be ignored.
issues.legal_principle: A party must prove the material facts supporting its title, and a document that lacks identifying information necessary to connect it to the disputed property cannot establish that title. The Court also applied the principle that a court cannot travel beyond the pleadings.

predicates.civil_title_proceeding: A party brings a civil proceeding to establish ownership of property.
predicates.a_party_relies_on_a_rent_document_to_pro: A party relies on a rent or lease document as evidence of ownership of the disputed property.
predicates.the_document_does_not_identify_the_prope: The document omits information needed to identify the land, the parties, or the material terms of the arrangement.

issues.definition: A rent document that does not identify the disputed property or the relevant parties or terms does not establish title in a civil title proceeding.
